No. Appending passes to that log would not make the revised draft checked, and I would not call it checked on that basis.

Why not

A checks.jsonl log is a record of what was checked, against which version of the draft, and against which citation inventory. Your draft and inventory both changed after the log was created. That leaves the existing entries in one of three states:

- They describe text or citations that no longer exist in the draft.
- They describe text that still exists but now sits in a changed context. Examples are a moved quotation, an edited proposition, or a pincite that now supports a different sentence.
- They are untouched and still accurate, but nothing in the log tells you which entries those are.

If you add new "pass" lines on top of that, a reader of the log will see a clean run. They will have no way to tell which lines were checked against the old draft and which against the new one. A pass that was never run against the current draft is a false record, and that is worse than having no log.

The next step

1. Freeze the revised draft. Treat the current text as the version you are checking, and record an identifier for it, such as a file hash or a version label and date.
2. Rebuild the citation inventory from the revised draft rather than editing the old one. Compare it with the old inventory so you know what was added, removed, or altered. That comparison tells you where to focus, but it does not replace a full re-check.
3. Start a new log for the revised draft, or archive the old one and mark it superseded. The new log should name the draft version and inventory version it covers. Do not mix old and new entries in one file.
4. Re-run every check against the revised draft. You may carry an old result forward only if you re-verify that the underlying text and citation are unchanged. Record it as carried forward with the reason, not as a fresh pass.
5. Resolve every failure, open item, and item marked as needing verification before you use the word "checked." If any citation has not been confirmed against its source, say so in the log and in what you tell others, for example "checked except items X and Y."
6. Make any further edit a new version. If you edit the draft again after the new log is complete, the log is stale again, and you repeat the process.

A caution about me

I cannot run checks, open files, or look up authorities in this conversation. I have not checked your draft or your log, and I cannot confirm any pass. Everything above is about process. The checking itself has to be done by you, or by a tool or person with access to the draft and to the cited sources.

Wording you can use until then: "The revised draft has not yet been checked. The prior log applies only to the earlier version."
